title: Four lines (section 8)
hook: teaching even four lines of this sutra is worth more than worlds full of treasure

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing fixed: there's no fixed thing called the highest awakening. Your line: nothing fixed.

Treasure enough to fill a world. Then another world, and another, until a whole vast system of worlds is heaped with gold and silver and jewels. Someone gives every bit of it away. The Buddha asks Subhuti: would that giver's merit be great? Very great, Subhuti says. Of course. Then the Buddha sets something on the other side of the scale, small enough to fit on an index card.
screen: `WORLDS HEAPED WITH TREASURE.` → `ALL OF IT GIVEN AWAY.` → `SOMETHING ON THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the scale. On one side, a world system filled with treasure, all of it given away. Subhuti agrees that's great merit, and adds a twist in the sutra's usual way: it's great because merit, too, isn't a fixed thing. Second, the other side. If someone takes up even a verse of four lines from this sutra, keeps it, and explains it to others, the Buddha says, that merit is greater. Not the whole sutra. Four lines, kept and passed on. Third, the reason. All the Buddhas, and their highest awakening, the sutra says, come out of this teaching. Teaching is where Buddhas come from, so passing even a little of it on outweighs the treasure. Then, right away, the sutra cuts its own praise: what is called the Buddha's teaching is not the Buddha's teaching. Even what it just lifted up gets no place to settle. Fourth, which four lines? The sutra doesn't say. Some readers point to the short verses this sutra contains. Others say it means any four lines of it, so the smallest piece is enough. Either way, the measure isn't size. A verse said to one person at a kitchen table counts. And notice who does the work: not the one who reads silently and keeps it to themselves, but the one who keeps it and explains it to someone else. Four lines can be a text message, a sticky note on a mirror, or what you say to a friend at a bad moment, when you remember something that once helped you.
screen: `WORLDS FULL OF TREASURE.` · `EVEN FOUR LINES, PASSED ON.` · `WHERE THE BUDDHAS COME FROM.` · `WHICH FOUR? THE SUTRA DOESN'T SAY.` · then, large: `FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: Let four lines come to mind that once helped you: a verse, a saying, a few words someone said that stayed, from a sutra or not. Let one rise on each out-breath, all four, then begin again. As they go round, don't plan anything; just let a face come, someone who might need them, and rest in the breath.
Four lines. Even a verse of four lines from this sutra, kept and explained to others, outweighs worlds of treasure given away. Today's word.
Your line: four lines. Small enough to carry, heavier than worlds. Rest well.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities, short passages of the Diamond Sutra are copied, recited and shared, and teachers point to this section when explaining why passing a teaching on is counted as merit.

myth: the sutra names exactly which four lines it means
it doesn't say. some readers point to its verses; others say any four lines.
in section eight, four lines kept and explained outweigh worlds of treasure given away
the Buddha says that merit is greater.
the sutra says giving treasure earns no merit

fork.setup: you've just read four lines of this sutra that stayed with you. by the sutra's own measure, what makes them count for the most?
options: keeping them and explaining them to someone else.
buying a beautiful copy to keep them in.
fork.reveal: the sutra praises the one who keeps even four lines and explains them to others: that merit outweighs worlds of treasure.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: a verse; the sutra praises even a verse of four lines.

trapdoor: what you thought: four lines is a magic number, like a spell.
what it means: even a short verse of this teaching, kept and explained to someone, outweighs worlds of treasure given away.
what a scholar hears: gatha, a verse. the sutra praises passing it on, then says the Buddha's teaching is not the Buddha's teaching, so even the praise can't be grasped.
guess: a short verse, kept and shared, outweighs worlds of gifts
a short prayer said four times before each meal
the four rules every monk keeps before teaching

chat.says: Why would a few lines of a sutra matter more than giving away a fortune?
options: Buddhas come from this teaching, the sutra says, so four lines passed on weigh more.
The sutra says giving away treasure earns no merit at all, so anything beats it.
Reading four lines silently to yourself is worth more than any gift, it says.
chat.meaning: The sutra says all Buddhas come out of this teaching, so even four lines kept and explained outweigh worlds of treasure.

Subhuti.meaning: the disciple who questions the Buddha in this sutra

merit.meaning: the good that comes from good deeds

world system.meaning: a vast cluster of worlds, in Buddhist cosmology

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text.

All wording paraphrased (quoted: null). The sutra's 'three thousand great thousand worlds' and 'seven treasures' are rendered as 'a whole vast system of worlds' and 'gold and silver and jewels' under the claims rule.
'Which four lines' is left open in the voice; confirm the two readings described (the sutra's own verses vs any four lines) are fair to the commentary tradition.
Subhuti's twist ('merit, too, isn't a fixed thing') paraphrases the line that the merit is great because it is not merit; check wording.
